Many people are aware that modern computing has its roots in Alan Turing, who designed the machine that broke Germany's "Enigma" code and helped win WW2. But few people know of the philosophical developments that occurred in England and led to Turing's project. Ludwig Wittgenstein was a professor of Turing (and interestingly one of Adolph Hitler's classmates), and wrote the mystical Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus which rocked the intellectual community of England and wherein he proved that:

"For an answer which cannot be expressed, the question too cannot be expressed." "The riddle does not exist." "If a question can be put at all, then it can also be answered."

Wittgenstein not only proved that any code can be broken, he proved that any question that can be asked can also be answered, via logical computation. If there's no answer possible, then it really isn't a question at all, it is literally non-sense.

The Turing machine is the most powerful computer possible, capable of, if given enough time, answering any question that can be asked. All computers built since just have faster processing speeds and optimizations for common computations. The infamous "Halting Problem" concerns the issue of answering the question of whether the machine will ever produce an answer to another question you posed, which is to say whether or not the other "question" is really a question at all. If it is a real question, then the machine will answer it, eventually. But if the machine is still processing, you can't be certain whether it will ever answer it, or it just needs more time; it can't tell you beforehand whether you asked it a real question.

And furthermore, with careful study we might be able to map computational functions onto naturally occurring physical systems, beings and phenomena - there might be naturally occurring Turing machines that could be consulted and interpreted by experts who through close observation learned their patterns and operation.

What this means is that ancient civilizations very likely had their own machines.
